text: Now we come to the other scenario. This is when a leading citizen becomes the prince of his country, not through wickedness or intolerable violence, but through the favor of his fellow citizens. We can call this a civil principality. You do not need absolute genius or pure luck to achieve this, but rather a lucky kind of shrewdness. I argue that you obtain this kind of principality through the favor of either the people or the nobles. Every city contains these two distinct groups. They exist because the people do not want to be ruled or oppressed by the nobles, while the nobles desperately want to rule and oppress the people. These two opposing desires inevitably lead to one of three results in a city: a principality, a free republic, or total anarchy.

A principality is created by either the people or the nobles, depending on which group seizes the opportunity. When the nobles realize they cannot defeat the masses, they start building up the reputation of one of their own. They make him a prince so they can pursue their selfish ambitions while hiding behind his authority. On the other hand, when the people realize they cannot resist the nobles, they elevate one of their own to power. They make him prince so his authority can protect them. A man who gains power with the help of the nobles will have a much harder time keeping it than one who rises through the support of the people. The prince backed by nobles is surrounded by men who consider themselves his equal. Because of this, he can neither rule them nor manage them as he pleases. But a man who comes to power through the favor of the people stands alone. He has very few people around him, if any, who will refuse to obey his commands.

Furthermore, it is impossible to satisfy the nobles fairly without injuring others, but you can easily satisfy the people. The goal of the people is far more righteous than that of the nobles. The nobles want to oppress, while the people simply want to avoid oppression. Add to this the fact that a prince can never secure himself against a hostile public because there are simply too many of them. He can, however, secure himself against the nobles, because they are few in number. The worst a prince can expect from a hostile public is that they will abandon him. But with hostile nobles, he must fear not only abandonment, but outright rebellion. The nobles are far-seeing and astute. They will always act in time to save themselves, seeking favors from whoever they believe will win. Finally, a prince is forced to live with the exact same common people forever. But he can do perfectly fine without the same nobles, as he has the power to create and destroy them every single day, granting or stripping away their authority whenever it suits him.

To make this crystal clear, you should evaluate the nobles in two primary ways. Either they conduct themselves in a way that ties their fate entirely to yours, or they do not. Those who bind themselves to you, provided they are not excessively greedy, should be honored and loved. Those who refuse to bind themselves to you must be handled in two different ways. Sometimes, they do this out of cowardice and a natural lack of courage. In this case, you should make use of them, especially those who offer good advice. This way, they will bring you honor in times of prosperity, and you will not have to fear them in times of adversity. But other times, they refuse to tie themselves to you out of sheer ambition. This is a clear warning sign. It proves they are thinking more about their own interests than yours. A prince must guard against these men and treat them like open enemies, because the moment you face a crisis, they will eagerly help to destroy you.

Therefore, a man who becomes prince through the favor of the people must keep them friendly. This is easy to do, since they only ask that he does not oppress them. But a man who becomes prince through the favor of the nobles, against the will of the people, has one ultimate priority. Above everything else, he must seek to win the people over to his side. He can do this easily by taking them under his protection. When men receive good treatment from someone they expected to harm them, they feel a much stronger loyalty to their benefactor. As a result, the people will quickly become even more devoted to him than if he had gained power through their support in the first place. A prince can win their affection in many different ways. These methods change depending on the specific situation, so I cannot lay down fixed rules for them, and I will leave them out. But I will repeat this one absolute necessity: a prince must keep the people friendly, otherwise he will have zero security when disaster strikes.

Consider Nabis, the prince of the Spartans. He survived a combined attack from all of Greece and a victorious Roman army. Against overwhelming odds, he defended both his country and his government. To survive this extreme peril, he only needed to secure himself against a small handful of internal enemies. If the general public had been hostile to him, stopping those few enemies would never have been enough. Do not try to argue against my point with that tired old proverb:
He who builds on the people, builds on mud.

That saying is only true for a private citizen who relies on the masses, fooling himself into believing the people will rescue him if he is targeted by enemies or magistrates. A man like that will find himself severely disappointed. This is exactly what happened to the Gracchi brothers in Rome, and to Messer Giorgio Scali in Florence. But imagine a true prince who builds his foundation on the people. He is a man who knows how to command and possesses real courage. He does not panic in the face of adversity. He takes the necessary precautions, and through his sheer resolution and energy, he keeps the spirit of the entire population alive. A prince like this will never be betrayed by his people, and the world will see that he has laid his foundations perfectly.

Civil principalities face their greatest danger when they transition from a civil government to absolute rule. These absolute princes either rule directly, or they rule through public magistrates. If they rule through magistrates, their government is significantly weaker and more insecure. The prince's power rests entirely on the goodwill of the citizens appointed to those offices. During troubled times, these magistrates can destroy the government with incredible ease, either through secret plotting or open defiance. When the chaos begins, the prince will not have the chance to seize absolute authority. The citizens and subjects are used to taking orders from the magistrates, and they will refuse to obey the prince in the middle of a crisis. In times of doubt, the prince will always face a desperate shortage of men he can trust. A prince in this situation cannot rely on what he sees during quiet, peaceful times. When the state is running smoothly and the citizens need the government, everyone agrees with him. Everyone makes grand promises. When death is a distant thought, they all swear they would die for him. But when times get tough and the state actually needs its citizens, the prince will find almost no one willing to stand by him. This transition to absolute power is incredibly dangerous, especially because you only get to try it once. Therefore, a wise prince must design a system where his citizens will always need the state, and always need him, no matter the circumstances. If he does this, they will remain faithful forever.
